newsitem.title: ITALY: INTERVIEW-Benetton prepares for steady lira.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Benetton prepares for steady lira.

text.p: Benetton is facing up to a new potential challenge -- living with a steady lira.

The fashion clothing manufacturer has traditionally had 80 percent of its costs based in lira and two-thirds of its sales are outside Italy, so the lira's fall over the last four years has clearly benefitted the Italian group.

Benetton's managing director Carlo Gilardi believes Benetton is ready for the challenge of a more stable lira after the Italian currency re-entered Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) in November 1996 after a four-year absence.

"We have increased our market share, increased our efficiencies and competitiveness when the lira was weak and even decreased some prices. When the lira is stable this will not affect Benetton," he said in a interview.

Benetton has lived with a situation that when the lira was weak its operating profits grew and it lost on its hedging policy, while the lira turned strong Benetton's operating profit suffered and the group gained on its hedging profits.

Benetton first half 1996 profits showed all the signs of lira strength -- turnover was flat in lira terms, operating profits were squeezed 12.1 percent lower but foreign exchange earnings from hedging made 39.4 billion lire ($23 million) versus a loss of 22.8 billion in the first half of 1995.

For the full 1996 year, foreign exchange profits may well double, analysts say. But for Benetton this picture would steady into 1997 and towards the start of the European single currency scheduled to start in 1999.

One thing Gilardi is clear about is that the vast majority of production will remain in Italy where Benetton's investment in technology outweighs possible cheaper labour available elsewhere, and there will only be miminium production abroad.

Benetton's Italian system of sub-contracting all labour intensive clothing assembly while it retains control of essential material purchase, cutting, dying and distribution keeps costs contained with a direct workforce of only 6,000.

Sparkling new new factories around its home town of Ponzano near Treviso, some 50 km (30 miles) north of Venice, and a computer-controlled warehouse delivering to its global 7,000 licensed shops keep efficiencies high.

Gilardi is not to be tempted into moving substantial manufacturing to the Far East, such as has happened at the rapidly-growing U.S. clothing group GAP. "We are manufacturers, they are retailers," says Gilardi.
Benetton sells to its licensed retail outlets at wholesale prices, while San Francisco-based GAP contracts its manufacturing out to focuses on its own retail outlets.

GAP is very strong in its own backyard of the U.S. and has only started its European expansion. Still in GAP's homeland, Benetton has not made a profit since 1988 despite annual sales of over 200 billion lire.
Gilardi says Benetton's strategy is to stay in America and it is performing there fairly well. "We don't want to be first in America, we want to be first all over the world.
